I. Summary
Final Decisions (FDs) dated June 15, 2020, and issued by the Field Manager of
the Jarbidge Field Office (JFO), Bureau of Land Management (BLM), have been
appealed by one or more of the following entities: Camas Creek Cattle Association
LLC, Winter Grazing LLC, and Grassy Hills LLC (collectively known as Camas
Creek Ranch) and JRS Properties III LLLP dba Cedar Creek Cattle (JRS) (hereinafter
all referred to as the Permittees). The FDs renew, with modifications, the Permittees’
grazing permits for grazing allotments (Allotments) in south-central Idaho within
the Devil Creek Subregion of the JFO’s jurisdiction (JFO Area).
Now pending are BLM’s Motion for Summary Judgment (Camas Creek and
JRS Properties) and the Permittees’ Motion for Partial Summary Judgment.1 BLM’s
motion is about all the appeals’ claims and Allotments except two, the Pigtail Butte
and Coonskin-EJD Allotments.2 The Permittees move for summary judgment on
most claims and assert that summary judgment is not appropriate on other claims
because there are genuine issues of material fact.
Historically, the Devil Creek Subregion was vegetated with sage-
shrub/bunchgrass vegetation communities. Its vegetation has been converted to
primarily grasslands without adequate sagebrush cover, mainly because of repeated
wildfires and post-fire seedings with crested wheatgrass. In addition, non-native

annual grasses, like cheatgrass, are common and provide fine fuels that exacerbate
wildfire spread.
One of the management objectives of the 2015 Jarbidge Record of Decision
and Approved Resource Management Plan (2015 RMP) and the FDs is to convert
some of the grasslands back to shrublands. Therefore, the FDs increase grazing
levels, sometimes substantially, to increase utilization levels and expand livestock
distribution to reduce non-native plant species and other fine fuels. Doing this
creates opportunities for extant shrub communities to expand.
The Permittees narrowly focus on this objective in arguing that the FDs and
BLM’s supporting environmental analysis violated the National Environmental
Policy Act (NEPA) and the Federal Land Policy Management Act (FLPMA). They
argue that BLM violated NEPA because the scientific literature does not show that
the increases in utilization levels and other grazing management authorized in the
FDs will reduce fine fuels and accelerate sagebrush recruitment and, even if the
literature did, the permittees cannot actually elevate the utilization levels in light of
certain grazing management parameters, including variations in pasture
characteristics, the water supply, and the FD’s schedules for deferring pastures.
Based on these arguments, they also argue that BLM violated the 2015 RMP
objective to convert grassland to shrubland and FLPMA.
But the Permittees have not marshalled the scientific literature and grazing
parameters to adequately support their arguments. Further, the following facts do
not favor a finding that the 2015 RMP objective and FLPMA were violated: (1) the
RMP-specified timeframe for meeting this objective exceeds the 10-year duration of
the grazing permits, (2) grazing management only has a limited role in meeting this
objective, and (3) the FDs are designed to meet many other objectives, including
competing 2015 RMP objectives.
Ultimately, the Permittees have failed to provide specific facts showing that
there is a genuine issue of material fact. The undisputed material facts show that
BLM is entitled to summary judgment. Therefore, BLM’s motion for summary
judgment is granted, the Permittees’ motion for partial summary judgment is
denied, and the pending appeals are dismissed, except those appeals relating to the
Coonskin-EJD and Pigtail Butte Allotments. Also, I make simple modifications to
some of the FDs using 43 C.F.R. § 4.479(d).

II. Factual Background
The JFO Area is made up of 1.4 million acres of public and private lands in
southern Idaho and northern Nevada.3 The area includes 911,000 acres of habitat for
the Greater sage-grouse, a BLM special status species, 600,000 acres of which has
been burned by wildfire in recent years.4
This includes about 284,160 acres (almost 80 percent) of the 357,816 acres of
BLM-managed lands in Devil Creek Subregion that burned at least once between
1993 and 2013. Thus, while much of the subregion was historically populated with
sagebrush steppe plant communities, the subregion is currently dominated by
herbaceous vegetation because of past fire and post-fire grass and forb seeding or
natural recovery of native or seeded species. In other words, wildfire is the primary
factor influencing vegetation composition and wildlife habitats in the subregion.5
Some shrub reestablishment is occurring where shrubs were seeded or
planted post-fire and via natural recruitment where seed sources are present. That
said, sagebrush growth and recruitment are slow, even when facilitated by seeding
or planting; sagebrush community reestablishment is a process that requires several
decades and the absence of additional fire.6
The sagebrush steppe ecosystem present in the JFO Area features sagebrush
in the overstory; native grasses, forbs, and litter in the understory; and biological soil
crusts filling interspaces between vegetation. Biological soil crusts play critical
ecological roles in the sage-steppe. These include promoting nitrogen fixation and
nutrient cycling; protecting soils from wind and water erosion; resisting alien plant
invasions; and reducing the spread and intensity of wildfire. These crusts are
vulnerable to trampling from livestock, especially in the winter and spring when the
crusts are moist. Native grass and forb communities of the sagebrush-steppe also

Sage-grouse depend on large, contiguous areas of sagebrush habitat that
support adequate shrub canopy cover and perennial grass and forb understories for
breeding, nesting, brood-rearing, and wintering. Sage-grouse hens usually place
their nests under sagebrush, but also use other shrubs. Sage-grouse congregate on
communal strutting grounds (leks) to breed from March to early May. After
breeding, hens disperse into nesting areas around the leks, with the nesting season
beginning in mid- to late-April and extending into May or early June. Hens seek out
nest sites that are concealed from predators, especially avian, by a combination of
sagebrush and grass cover. An abundance of forbs is critical to the growth of young
sage-grouse.8
Livestock damage native grass and forb communities in various ways,
including by grazing during critical spring growth periods, which impairs their
vigor and reproductive success; trampling, breaking, and other physical impacts;
and the effects of preferential grazing by which livestock selectively graze on certain
more desirable species and thereby promote plant succession by less desirable
species. The combination of sagebrush, grasses, forbs, litter, and biological crusts in
the sagebrush-steppe protects soils and resists erosion. By contrast, livestock
contribute to soil depletion and erosion in various ways, including by reducing
native plant vigor and presence, damaging soil crusts, and exposing and disturbing
soils. They also foster the spread of annual invasive plants, including cheatgrass
which is one of the leading causes of the heightened fire danger in the JFO Area.9

agreed to (1) undertake a revision of the 1987 Jarbidge Rangeland Management Plan

In 2007, the Murphy Complex Fire burned over 400,000 acres in the JFO Area,
destroying massive amounts of sagebrush habitat used by the sage-grouse,
including 70 percent of the remaining nesting habitat.11 After WWP requested
reopening the lawsuit to ban grazing in numerous allotments with key unburned
habitat for sage-grouse and other imperiled species in serious decline, the Court
issued a 2009 Order that included the following finding of fact:
To avoid conflicting with sage grouse mating, nesting and brood
rearing, grazing should be limited around leks and nests to . . . periods
between June 20 and August 1 (so that grazing is not occurring during
the mating and nesting seasons discussed above) and between
November 15 and March 1 (when plant growth has ceased for the
year).[ 12]
In September 2015, BLM issued the 2015 RMP. The planning area of the 2015
RMP is divided into four different Vegetation Management Areas (VMAs).13 The
Upland Vegetation section of the 2015 RMP contains objectives for VMAs B and C—
the VMAs where the subject Allotments are located.14 In light of the recent history of
large and repeated wildfires that resulted in conversion of much of the Devil Creek
Subregion from sagebrush steppe to grassland vegetation communities, those
objectives include changing the acreages of vegetative communities as follows: (1)
reduce annual communities by 29,000, (2) reduce non-native perennial communities
by 155,000, (3) reduce native grassland communities by 218,000, and (4) increase
native shrubland communities by 354,000.15 In other words, the focus of these
objectives is to convert grassland to shrubland (hereinafter referred to as the
“Conversion Objectives”).

One way to do so is for BLM to take interim steps to reduce fine fuels and to
open spaces in dense grassland communities to allow sagebrush to spread. Thus, in
the 2015 RMP, BLM increased its livestock allocation from about 189,000 animal unit
months (AUMs) in the 1987 RMP to up to about 326,000 AUMs. This was done in
response to data showing forage available for livestock under the vegetation
allocations and light levels of utilization. Grazing levels are expected to decline over
the life of the plan, as shrub-dominated vegetative communities expand.16
A week after its issuance, the 2015 RMP was amended by the Idaho and
Southwestern Montana Greater Sage-Grouse Approved Resource Management Plan
Amendment (2015 ARMPA).17 BLM and the U.S. Forest Service developed the 2015
ARMPA in response to the 2010 finding by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS)
under the Endangered Species Act that listing the Greater sage-grouse was
warranted but precluded for listing due to higher agency priorities.18 Sagebrush
habitat—which is critically important to sage-grouse as a sagebrush obligate—and
sage-grouse populations have experienced serious long-term and short-term
declines throughout the sage-grouse’s range, including the Devil Creek Subregion
and the rest of the JFO Area.19 One of the 2015 ARMPA’s goals is to conserve,
enhance, and restore the sagebrush ecosystem upon which the sage-grouse
populations depend in an effort to maintain and/or increase their abundance and
distribution.20
In 2016, BLM began to fully process new grazing permits by dividing the 1.4-
million-acre JFO Area into subregions based on similar geographic characteristics
and resource issues.21 As part of BLM’s permit renewal process for the Devil Creek
Subregion, a BLM interdisciplinary team (ID Team) prepared Rangeland Health
Assessments and Evaluation Reports (RHAs) to determine whether the grazing
allotments and pastures were meeting the Idaho Standards for Rangeland Health
(Standards). As part of this process, BLM collected field data and requested relevant

The RHAs were issued in August 2019, along with an initial environmental
assessment (Initial EA) that evaluated the impacts of renewing livestock grazing

Allotments.29 In the Initial EA, BLM considered nine alternatives and analyzed these
six alternatives in detail:
• Alternative 1 – Current Management: Alternative 1 carried forward all
allotment management, including average annual AUMs from 2004 through
2015, livestock numbers, seasons of use, grazing systems, terms and
conditions, and monitoring, for the allotments over the past 10 years. No new
range infrastructure was contemplated under this alternative.
• Alternative 2 – Permittee Proposed Action: Alternative 2 was based on the
Permittees’ proposals in their grazing applications and included increased
AUMs, new or modified range infrastructure, and allotment or pasture
boundary adjustments. Under this alternative, the most miles of new fences,
miles of new water pipeline, and new water troughs would be constructed
and construction of the range infrastructure projects would disturb the most
acreage: 585 acres.

• Alternative 3 – Vegetative Production: Alternative 3 included AUM increases
based on the most current vegetative production data and the method used
for forage allocation in the 2015 RMP. The increases would be phased in over
three to five years. For flexibility, grazing may take place any time during the
year, with seasons of use, livestock numbers, pasture rotations, and active
AUMs—subject to AUM and livestock number limits—determined in annual
grazing plans (AGPs) developed in coordination with the Permittees and
based on monitoring data review.
Relatedly, Alternative 3 provided for adaptive management in the
form of Objectives (O’s), Management Guidelines (Guidelines or MGs),
Thresholds (TH’s), Grazing Systems (GS’s), and Monitoring assigned to each
pasture. The Objectives included maintaining and improving native plant
species diversity and abundance, focusing on plant reproductive and
physiological needs; accelerating sagebrush restoration by reducing fine fuels
and herbaceous competition; and maintaining properly functioning condition
(PFC) in riparian and wetland areas or improving conditions to achieve or
make progress towards achieving PFC. The Guidelines and Thresholds
included average end utilization limits for various vegetation communities,
with the Thresholds being higher than the Guidelines. Another adaptive
feature was a Response Toolbox of management options if Thresholds are
exceeded. And the Grazing Systems were three deferred rotation systems
where grazing would be deferred in a pasture from about March 1 through
July 15 every other year, every third year, or every two out of three years, and
two rest rotation systems where a pasture would be rested for the entire year
every other or every third year. This alternative included range infrastructure
projects whose construction would disturb about 575 acres.
• Alternative 4 – Forage Availability and Resource Needs: Alternative 4
incorporated the vegetative production allocations as defined above for
Alternative 3 but adjusted AUMs for slope, distance to water, sage-grouse
breeding and nesting habitats, and other resource concerns. As under
Alternative 3, increases in AUMs would be phased in and adaptive
management would be used. This alternative includes range infrastructure
projects whose construction would disturb about 437 acres.
